Few dependencies (see [ENGINEERING.md](ENGINEERING.md)). | - Classify every remaining hunk as *contract* or *logic* with rules on its file's path: dependency manifests, schemas and migrations (an `openapi*` or `swagger*` file among them), CI and infrastructure, repository config, app config, and auth or security paths. A rule can only raise a hunk to *contract*; one no rule matches is *logic*. The rules read what a file is, never the names or text in it. A security path skips test code (tests, and helpers named fake, mock, stub or fixture), and doesn't make a hunk contract when every line it changes is inert: blank, a comment, an import, a string, an UPPER_CASE constant set to a literal, a closing bracket, or, in markup, a tag with literal attributes or plain text. The rules' contract is internal: it orders the flows, and the page never shows it. The model doesn't classify hunks, so a run changes no hunk's class; a risk pass that marked each one was the version before, and what it marked contract was a card on the page (see DESIGN.md). Line rules were the version before that: credential storage and authorization read from the shape of a name (`save_secret`, `require_permission`), credential endpoints from a changing route with a `token`-like segment, risky calls from regexes on added lines (`eval(`, `subprocess`, `shell=True`), and removed or skipped tests from counts of declarations and skip markers. Probed with counterexamples, each failed both ways: a lexer's `clear_tokens()`, `Notification.requestPermission()`, `POST /llm/tokens`, "subprocess" in a log message and two tests merged into one were contract, while `localStorage.setItem("token", …)`, a removed owner check, a removed `@login_required`, `POST /login`, `spawn("sh", ["-c", cmd])`, `pickle.loads`, a deleted assertion and `@unittest.skip` were logic. Risk is about behavior, what a check guards, what a response exposes, what an assertion still proves, and a name doesn't say it; longer word lists only move the edges. What a name can't say is the findings pass's, with Request AI review. On delphi-code #2 the line rules made 10 hunks contract and path rules alone make 3: keychain.py, on a security path, and openapi.json's two. Only when the reviewer asks, on the **model option** they choose: a model on a provider, which is what runs the passes and decides who pays. The same model on two providers is two options, since the bill differs. A provider answers its own status and its options, and the list is their answers together: Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 on Claude Code, then the same three on the Anthropic API, then GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Sol on Codex, those of them the reviewer's `codex debug models` lists, then every chat model the reviewer's opencode offers, grouped by the provider behind it. One list of models, with the provider picked for them, was the alternative; it hides who pays, which is what a reviewer chooses by. A model is listed once the evals have run on it, with its scores in a report under `evals/reports/`, because the prompts were tuned on Haiku and a wrong finding costs the reviewer more than a missed one; listing every model a provider serves was the alternative. opencode's are the exception: they're whatever the reviewer connected, and the evals can't run on all of them, so every one is listed, marked unmeasured; listing only models measured elsewhere would leave out local models, the reason to use opencode. The analysis records the option its run used, and the page names it (see UI); Remove AI review and a new run is how another model is tried on the same PR. One option runs every pass, with the same prompts: a model per pass, or prompts per model, would each be a model the evals haven't measured. The default, when the reviewer hasn't chosen, is **Sonnet 5.5** (`claude-sonnet-5-5`) on the first provider that can run it. On the 14 eval cases through Claude Code it met 9 of the 12 targets against Haiku's 7: no wrong findings where Haiku had 21% (6 of 28), 7% of its decisions noise against 36%, and every contract hunk marked where Haiku missed 4 of 25 (`evals/reports/2026-11-14/`). It was faster too, about 3.5 minutes for the run against 6, because it writes a quarter of Haiku's output tokens. Those evals had the risk and decisions passes, which are gone since. It costs about 4× Haiku at API prices, $0.17 a case against $0.04, and on a plan more of its usage limits. Haiku stays the default was the alternative; the cost is still cents a PR, and the menu offers Haiku to a reviewer who wants it. Opus 5.5 met 8 targets at more than twice Sonnet's cost. Each Claude model's ID, name, price, input budget, output limit under each transport and the efforts it accepts are in one table in the adapter, `src/adapters/model/claude/models.ts`, and each OpenAI model's slug, name and price in `src/adapters/model/codex/models.ts`, its context window and efforts coming from Codex's catalog; a pass whose effort a model doesn't accept runs at the nearest one it does. The prompts, input rendering, output schema and pass model every provider shares are in `src/adapters/model/shared/`, apart from Claude's transports, so a provider imports only those, never another provider; the dependency rules check it. - **Codex,** for OpenAI's models: one `codex exec` per pass, on the reviewer's ChatGPT plan. Each runs without a shell in a new empty directory, with our instructions in place of Codex's (`model_instructions_file`, which also saves about 4,300 tokens a call), the answer's schema as `--output-schema`, the read-only sandbox, `--ephemeral` so the review isn't in the reviewer's Codex history, and none of their config, rules or `AGENTS.md`. The answer is the last message's text, parsed as JSON and then with the same Zod schema. Its size check estimates 3 bytes a token after 6,000 of Codex's own, where the eval cases measured 3.36 to 5.19 bytes and about 5,300 tokens, against the model's context window less 32,000 for the answer. Codex reports tokens and no cost, so the cost is computed at OpenAI's API prices, or absent for a model without one. The findings read the intent's answer, to name the mismatch a finding shows, and the steps pass reads no other's. The intent pass starts first and writes the PR to the prompt cache, and the findings start when it ends. The steps pass starts as soon as the intent's answer begins, when the PR is in the cache, and reads it from there; Claude Code says so with the model's first message, the API with the stream's first event, and Codex and opencode say nothing until the answer is done, so there it waits for the intent to end. On Claude Code the model's first message comes as its thinking ends, a moment before the answer, so both start about when the intent ends. A risk and a decisions pass ran beside the steps until the risk and decision points went (see DESIGN.md). Every pass starting at once was tried: each wrote the whole PR to the cache, and on the evals the passes cost 2.5 times as much at API prices, $2.27 against $0.78 on delphi-code #2. Intent is kept short, because the reviewer reads it before any code: each summary is one sentence, with at most 5 behavior changes. The inferred intent's summary is the header's brief, at most 20 words that don't repeat the title. What the code does that nobody asked for, or does differently, is a mismatch even when the summary leaves it out, and the prompt says so; what changes for existing code or data isn't, which naming it beside them made one on the evals, two more false mismatches on the baseline's 24 cases. It said it of the brief's watch line while the pass wrote one, a shape and at most 2 things to watch beside the summary: without it, on the evals' large-retry-after the brief said the unrequested body-read timeouts and the pass reported no mismatch, in two runs of two, so nothing marked the code. The page stopped showing the two, and the pass stopped writing them; an analysis stored with them parses without them. The findings pass reads the intent's summary and mismatches. The findings pass is the model's job: triage. It looks for three types of finding, each with a bar, an example that counts and one that doesn't: a contract finding names what breaks outside the PR and shows it, and an architecture finding names the code in the data it goes against, one of three things (see DESIGN.md). A finding is one type, contract when it's also another. It lists at most 10, most important first, and only what the code in the data shows, because a wrong finding costs the reviewer more than a missed one. The server checks that each one's hunk exists and that the hunk shows its lines; one still wrong after the retry is dropped and logged. A finding posts as the reviewer's comment, so the prompt asks for plain words: what happens rather than the class of problem it belongs to, a technical term only where it's the exact name, short sentences, and the code's own names and values kept, since plain isn't vague. Told only to write to the author in 300 characters, Sonnet wrote "`beforeThreadRun` callocs `ALLOCATION_BYTES`", "a privilege escalation" and "a privacy and compliance decision", which the author has to translate and the reviewer to reword before posting. On the evals it found what it did before, with fewer long words and asides (`evals/reports/2026-11-25/`). A second model call that rewrites the findings was the alternative: seconds on every run, and a rewrite can change what a finding says after the server checked it. A setting for the tone was the other, a choice nobody needs to make. A risk's reason and a decision had the same words asked of them while they were points, after their tasks and never changing what was decided. A title or explanation longer than the prompt asks is kept as written, with no retry: on delphi-code #2 one explanation over 300 characters cost a second findings pass, 2 of the run's 5 minutes, and one still too long after the retry was dropped, a real finding lost for its length. A suggestion on base-side lines, which a comment can't replace, or a mismatch the intent doesn't have costs the finding only that, after the retry. The findings pass reads the intent's mismatches by ID, so one finding carries a mismatch it shows instead of the reviewer reading it twice. Matching them on the server by the hunk they rest on, so findings could start beside the intent, was tried: a hunk often holds two mismatches, and on the evals it gave description-contradicts' constant delay the mismatch about retrying 4xx errors. The passes read the **unchanged callers** the analysis has, as an `` block at the end of the PR data, in the text every pass shares and in the size check: each changed definition by name and the hunk that changes it, then each use with its file, line and the excerpt megareviewer keeps, escaped as PR content is, since it's code from the same repository. With none, nothing is written, and the text is byte for byte what it was, which a test holds. A run reads them from the analysis it starts from and never from a checkout, so a run that starts while the repository is downloading reads the PR without them. When the hunks fit only without the callers, the callers are left out after the files' contents, and a warning says so: a PR that could be read before they were isn't refused because of them. On the 24 eval cases, six of them made for the types, the first prompt tried found every contract and architecture must-have, with the label's type on 21 of 21 findings, none of 27 rated noise, and nothing on the two cases where an API or a credential is touched and nothing breaks (`evals/reports/2026-11-25/finding-types.md`). It's one run, and architecture is two small cases. The same answer holds the change's **data flow**, or none (`Analysis.dataFlow`, [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) says why the model writes it): where the data comes in, 2 to 7 stations in the order it moves, each with a name, when it runs, whether it keeps data, its changed files, what it hands the next and the changed files that only define that, and where the data ends up. `validateDataFlow` in the domain checks it against `dataFlowContext`, the pull request's paths and every pair of them a call-graph hint, a definition call, a request or an import joins: a file that isn't the pull request's or is placed twice, a station without a name or a file, stations past the seventh, and two neighbors nothing joins, counting what the first hands on. The problems go to the pass's one retry beside the steps'. After it `keptDataFlow` drops those files and stations and keeps neighbors nothing joins, which the page marks; fewer than two stations left is no flow. The flow stands by its own checks: an answer too small for a tour can have one, and a tour can have none. Its texts are mended of refs as a step's sentence is. The variant is in the union only a run that asks sends, so a run that doesn't sends what it did, and the transports' tour fingerprints moved with it; their prompt versions didn't, as when the pass was added. Claude Code took the union with the flow in one small call on Haiku 5.5 (`evals/union-check.ts`); no pass has written a flow of a real pull request yet. The union check of stage 64 found the Anthropic API refused the union as too large a grammar with the steps variant and without, which is why the API transport sends no format (see The Anthropic API above). What the reviewer values is kept in the store and given to the model passes as guidance. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) says what a preference is and why nothing learned applies by itself. **Measured.** The evals ran before and after the prompts learned to read guidance, on Sonnet 5.5 through Claude Code (`evals/reports/2026-11-17/guidance.md`). On the 14 cases without guidance no metric that met its target misses it now, and the risk metrics didn't move by a hunk in three runs. Decision noise was 4% before and 17% and 11% in two runs after, under its 20% target each time; the same prompts gave 0 to 4 noisy decisions of 5 to 7 on the three cases that moved, and the judge rated one unchanged decision both ways, so the runs don't show the prompt did it, and one run on the old prompts can't rule it out. Three cases have guidance: a tenant filter lost on one path with a Look for preference on tenant isolation, a paging bug beside a leftover `console.log` with a Don't flag on debug logging, and a migration with no down section under a `REVIEW.md` that asks for one. In three runs each, every expected mark came back and no other (`guidanceFollowed` 2 of 2, `leftOutRight` 6 of 6, `guidanceWrong` 0 of 5), and the bug beside the left-out `console.log` was found unmarked each time. What a Don't flag preference covers still reached the brief's watch line and its mismatches in three runs of three; a sentence for the intent task is proposed in stage 59's notes and isn't in. The guideline files at a PR's base commit and the files they link. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) says what's in it and why. `src/domain/review/harness.ts` reads links and plans what a run uses, `loadHarness` finds and stores one. **Links.** `harnessLinks` reads one file's: an `@path` after a space or at a line's start, as Claude Code reads an import; an inline or reference Markdown link; and any other path in prose. An import and a Markdown link are relative to their file, a Markdown link with a leading slash to the root, as both hosts render one. A path in prose can mean two files, since `docs/plan/README.md` in a root file and in `docs/notes.md` usually mean the same one, so it's tried against its file and then the root, and the first that's there is the link; trying only its file would lose most of a docs folder's, and taking both would add files nobody named. A code span is a path in prose when it holds a path and nothing else. A link to a path without an extension, or one ending in a slash, is to a folder, and outside a Markdown link only one ending in a slash is, so `@scope/package` and `I/O` cost no request; one that's a pattern, `docs/*.md`, isn't. A URL, a path under `~`, an absolute one, the root and one that leaves the repository aren't links. The patterns are linear in a file's size, which a test holds on a megabyte of brackets, backticks and dots. **One reader, of the harness's files.** What a pass can read is the run's harness files, under `harness/` at their repository paths, from the store and never from a checkout's working tree: where a command reads them, as regular files in a directory megareviewer writes, and on the API from memory. PR text can still ask for anything; the worst it gets is a team document from the base commit. A second root beside `harness/` is where code would go. An MCP server of ours was the first design, one handler on every transport, and no reader at all in an organization whose `managed-mcp.json` forbids added servers. **On Claude Code,** a pass that reads has a directory of its own, with the system prompt's file beside the one it runs in, not in it, `--tools "Read Grep"` and `--restricted`, which refuses a path outside the working directory, by `../` and through a link too, and `--max-turns` of 10: the rounds, one for the answer and a spare for one the schema refused. `claudeEnv` keeps Claude Code from loading a harness file named `CLAUDE.md` by itself, and lets one `Read` give 60,000 tokens, where a plain one stops at 25,000 without an error. Claude Code sends a use before it runs it, so megareviewer also resolves each path as it arrives, links followed, and kills the process on one outside or on any other tool. The kill is a check on the refusal, not the refusal. **On opencode,** a session that reads is given its directory and a rule for each file, `read` on that path, after the agent's denials. Leave for `read` on everything in the directory was the alternative: opencode resolves a path by its letters, and it read a file outside through a link, where a rule by name refused it. Not `grep`, whose rule takes a pattern and not a path, and which read the same file. A run's passes share one directory, since opencode puts its path ahead of the PR and passes in two would share no cache: on 69 files to read, through Haiku 5.5, each later pass read 174,257 tokens from it. Nothing tells an adapter that a run starts or ends, so the directory goes by the run's harness: the first pass writes it, the last one running removes it, and a later one has it written again at the same path, where nothing is, or runs without the reader. opencode loads an `AGENTS.md` beside a file it reads, or above it, by itself; that counts as a read when it's one of the harness's files, and fails the pass when it isn't. Renaming such a file in the copy was the alternative; the links to it would name nothing. A session's messages show while it runs, so megareviewer looks every 2 seconds and interrupts a pass at its ninth round; opencode's own limit, `steps`, writes the start of the last answer itself, which Haiku 5.5 refuses. What was read is checked on the turn, not killed: the permissions are what refuses, and a turn with more in it is discarded. A guardrail is a check that would catch a kind of problem before review, in any code. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) says why megareviewer names one, and where. **The guardrail call** is a model call of a run once its passes have ended, on the run's option, when the run has a finding. It reads the run's findings, those a Don't flag preference left out among them, each with the lines it rests on as its hunk shows them, at most 40 and the rest counted; the intent's mismatches no finding names aren't asked about. It reads too the check configs and build files at the PR's base commit through the file cache, for the languages of the files the points are in. A config's or build file's read that fails, or one over 32 KB, is a warning, and the call goes on without it. It runs on the one-call runner every transport has for the suggestion call (`RunOneCall`), with its own system prompt, schema and data in its one message, at medium effort; on opencode it's an agent of the server's config, `megareviewer-guardrails`, so opencode's prompt version moves with the call's prompt. The passes don't read configs: their system prompt, tasks, shared text and answer format are byte for byte what they were before the guardrail, and Claude Code's and Codex's prompt fingerprints are what they were then. The first version put a `` block in the passes' shared text and a `guardrail` field in the findings task, and asked again behind a button on a draft; the second grouped the reviewer's comments across pull requests and kept the groups in a table of its own. DESIGN.md says why both went. **The landing.** The passes end the run as before: their stages are done, the landing plays, and the review is there to read. When the call will run, the write that ends the last pass sets the analysis's `guardrails` to `running`, which isn't a stage, so the page's `inProgress` doesn't wait for it, and the passes' end is never announced as the run's: the events go on (`following`), that end announced as an update rather than `done`, and the call's end writes the marks and sends `done`, when the page reads the analysis again. Setting it in a write of its own after the passes was the alternative: the page could read the analysis between the two, see nothing running, and stop following before the marks. The marks then go in one render later than the rest (`useMarksHeld`), once the line of code at the top of the window is noted (`holdTopLine`), and that line is put back before the frame is painted, so a line opening on a card above it doesn't move the code being read; the landing doesn't play again, since it plays only on the run's own end. A failed call, an answer outside the schema or one over 30 seconds (`Clock.wait`, so tests control the time) leaves the review as the passes made it, `guardrails` `failed`, and the call's record saying why; with no finding there's no call, and `guardrails` stays null. A stop during the call fails it at the next start, as a stopped pass is. Remove AI review refuses while the call runs, as it does while the passes run. The call's usage and record are the run's, under the name `guardrails`: `ModelUsage.pass` and `ModelCall.pass` are a `ModelCallName`, the passes and the call, and the two passes since removed, so Run details lists it and the usage line counts it, and `ModelPass`, which every transport maps to a pass's prompt, is the passes there are. Through Claude Code on Sonnet 5.5 the call took 1.2 to 3.9 seconds on the eval cases, $0.004 to $0.015 at API prices (`evals/reports/2026-11-22/guardrail-call.md`). A guideline file that links others has a second line, “7 linked files, 88 KB” and how a review uses them, “2 in every review, 5 on request”, which opens to them by the file that links each, with a switch on each; a root that's off says what it would bring, “When on: …”, so the reviewer knows what switching `CLAUDE.md` on means before doing it. Folded, because megareviewer's own harness is 73 files and a list always open would bury the preferences above it. A linked file is on unless switched off, and one that's on behind a file that's off says “Ignored: links to it are off”; off by default was the first design, from before the reader, when a linked file cost the prompt its whole text rather than a line of the index. A guideline file another one links has no second switch, only its own row's, which shows on where an enabled root imports it. Under the list is what it doesn't have: a limit the links reached, each file too large or not text, and a load that isn't in. With none it says “None found at the repository's root.”, the five names it looks for behind an info button's tooltip and description rather than in the sentence. **Review page.** It opens on the code. The header names the PR once: its title, its number after it in grey, a link to it on the host, then the PR's state and its review status, and at the row's other end its CI and reviewers; one muted line of its repository, how much of it was read, who wants to merge which branch into which, when it was updated, and the lines it adds and removes, counted once the diff is read, a zero left out; and its intent as one line: what the change does. A line of the repository and number above the title, a count of threads beside it and the files in the byline were the version before: the bar's thread chip and the tree's file count said them again. Once Claude has run, a status line opens the brief, "✦ AI review · Sonnet 5.5 through Claude Code · latest commit", or "new commits since"; while it runs, "AI review running" and how many of the run's passes are done, three with the tour and two without, with a bar. It says only where the brief comes from: what can be done about it is in the bar. Its lead is semibold in the text's color, and only the check of "Does what was asked" is green; a green lead and a muted one were the version before, and read as two levels. It's Claude's once it has run, with the code names it writes in backticks set as code, as text, never as HTML. Before, it's the description's first sentence, with its Markdown markers dropped as plain text. Three lines were the version before: the run's Through and Watch under its summary, and before a run the code's own, from the overview's directories and the unchanged callers (see DESIGN.md). An info button, Details, ends the first line and opens the full intent in a dialog. The header scrolls away with the code. **How much of the repository was read** is an item of the byline, after the repository's name, once the code's stages are done: before that an analysis about to download says `none`, which would read as PR only for the seconds until the download starts. It's the analysis's `checkout` in three forms, each an icon and words: Whole repository for `read`, Downloading repository… with a spinner for `downloading`, and PR only, in the text's color and medium weight, for `none`, `missing-commit` and `download-failed`. It opens a popover. Read, it says how many uses outside the PR were found, tests among them, then the head commit and whether it was the reviewer's clone or megareviewer's own copy, its folder in a tooltip: "26 uses outside the PR. Read at `73432ec` from megareviewer's copy." A sentence naming the repository and the folder was the version before, three lines in the popover where the count, what the reviewer opens it for, came last. Otherwise it's the note the Details dialog ended with before, which a reviewer had to know was there: that it's downloading, or why nothing was read and what would fix it, now also that the repository wasn't downloaded because of `--no-download`. The status response's `downloadFolder`, the folder copies are downloaded to or null when that's off, tells a copy from a clone and says whether downloading is on; a folder under it is megareviewer's own. With downloading off a copy already there is still read, and is then named as a folder like any other. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) says why it always shows, and why not in the bar. Under it is the **bar**, one 52 px row that stays at the top of the window: the switch between the layouts, Claude's slot, Show files at 1024px or less, the reviewer's verdict on the host, then Approve and Publish. Once it's stuck it names the PR first, by its title, up to 384 px, and a divider. Each color in it means one thing: the primary as a tint is AI, filled it's committing a review, green is approving, red, orange and amber a finding's severity, and the rest is grey; at most one button is filled. `barButtons()` decides which: Publish while line comments wait for it, with their count; Approve once Claude's run is done and nothing waits, last on the row, unless the reviewer already approved or requested changes; neither before then, when the AI's tint is the row's strongest thing. Approve approves at once, with no dialog (see Publish). On the reviewer's own PR it's disabled, focusable and says why. New commits since the analysis don't disable it; it stays in outline then, beside Re-analyze's stronger tint. While the reviewer's approval stands it's Revoke approval instead, in outline and never disabled, and Publish shows only while comments wait. The verdict before the buttons is the reviewer's on the host, ✓ Approved, ✕ Changes requested or a speech mark and Commented, linking to the latest review published from the analysis when there is one; the PR's status says each reviewer's verdict, and the analysis view carries the reviewer's ID on the host (`currentUserId`) to find theirs. What the reviewer just did, an approval, a revocation or a review, sets it at once and holds until the status read after it answers, so the bar follows the click rather than a read that can fail (`verdictAfter`: a comment leaves an earlier approval or request for changes standing, as both hosts count them). While the status is unread it says "✓ Published" when a review was sent from here, which is all that's known. "✓ Published" always was the version before: it didn't say what the review was, and missed one given on the host's own page. The design blocked Approve while a finding was open; an open point means fine, so it doesn't. Claude's slot is what it found, the pager and the threads' chip, then after a divider the AI review's split button, never filled: before a run "✦ No AI review yet · Find bugs across 21 files" and Request AI review in the tint, its tooltip naming the model and who pays ("Runs Sonnet 5.5 through Claude Code, on your Pro plan") and, once the harness has loaded, what a run would read of it ("Reads CLAUDE.md and 3 files it imports; 66 more on request"), with nothing on it while it loads, when it couldn't be loaded, since the run loads it again and says what it's without, or when nothing is on; while it runs, a small "Reviewing · 1 of 3" with a spinner, not clickable; after it, a small Re-run in outline, which asks, takes the run off as Remove AI review does, and runs the chosen model again, the page following the new run from the analysis without loading it again; Try again after a run that didn't finish; and when the PR has new commits since the analysis, "Re-analyze · new commits" in a stronger tint, which starts a new analysis. A warning under the brief with Re-analyze was the version before. The design's Re-run counted the new commits and ran the AI again; new commits need a new analysis, and the status read doesn't count them. Its scope menu, the whole PR or the changes since the last review, was left out: a run can't cover only the changes. Beside the split's button a 28 px arrow in the same style opens the options grouped by provider, each group headed by what runs it and who pays or, when it can't, by why and the fix. An option that can't run is in the list, disabled, focusable and described by its group's reason; hiding it was the alternative, and a reviewer would never learn that signing in to the API adds options. A model the evals haven't measured, as every one of opencode's is, carries an "unmeasured" chip. Each group is one provider's options, or one provider's behind opencode, so its heading says what runs them and who pays. A group of more than six shows the chosen option and the default, else its first, and a field that filters the rest by every word typed, from which an arrow key goes to the option beside it rather than the menu's first; an Anthropic key alone gives opencode 20 models, which would outgrow the window. Showing them all, scrolled, was the alternative. The choice is kept per browser, as the Display menu's are, and sent with the run; one that can no longer run falls back to the default. The default is the option the last model call used, kept in the store, while it can run: the server listens on a new port at every start, a new origin whose browser storage is empty, so the choice alone put the reviewer back on Sonnet 5.5 after every restart. Keeping the choice only in the store was the alternative; a choice made in the menu without a run would then be lost on a reload. A settings page for the choice was the alternative, a page for one field, away from where the choice matters. While it runs, a hairline along the bar's bottom edge, and screen readers hear "Claude is reading this PR, 1 of 3 passes done"; the wording names the run's model family, read from the analysis, and the current choice's before a run, so it stays right when another provider's models are listed. "Claude is reading this PR" and the time since was the version before. Once it's done, the pager: one outlined group of segments split by a hairline, up to 576 px wide. Before the first step it's a bug, the count and an arrow, "3 findings ▾", which opens the list, and Start, which goes to the first; on a step, Previous and Next at its ends, the finding's severity glyph in its color and its title, which goes back to its card, and its position, "1 of 3 ▾", which opens the list. Previous and Next go round the points, every one a step, dismissed ones struck through, so the position doesn't jump when one is dismissed. The bar says "findings", in words and in the buttons' names, since a mismatch is labelled Finding on its card too. The list is a popover under the position, its rows in the pager's order with the current one marked, and when more than one type has findings a filter over them, "All 3 · ƒ logic 2 · ◆ contract 1": a type picked narrows the rows and what the arrows walk, and moves nothing on the page, and the position then says it, "1 of 2 logic ▾"; with All they walk every finding and the mismatches, which are of no type. Going to a point of another type, from the list's All or a mention, lets go of the filter. Three borderless words, `‹ 3 points ›`, with the current title after them as plain text and a chip per type before them, was the version before: the chips read as badges louder than the stepper, and nothing in the row looked like something to go through. The list was a dialog over a blurred page before; a popover keeps the code in view and the list where the reviewer clicked. Like the page's other popovers it doesn't trap the focus: Esc closes it back to the position, and Tab past its last row closes it and goes on to Next. The current point is the one last gone to, by the pager, the list, a mention or Raise, not the one in view. What a run didn't finish is named in the slot with why, and the split says Try again. Before the run the button's tint is the bar's strongest call to action, beside a Publish the reviewer has no reason to press yet; it was filled first, a second filled button once comments were pending. When no option can run, the button shows a lock, is disabled but stays focusable, and its tooltip, on hover or focus, and its description for screen readers give each provider's reason once ("Claude Code isn't signed in: run `claude` and sign in; or No Anthropic API credentials: …"); the arrow still opens the list. An enabled button whose click failed with that reason was the version before: the reviewer learned why only by trying. Analyze with Claude was its name first; Request AI review is the design's, and says what the reviewer gets rather than what runs it, which the tooltip says. Next at the end of the intent line was the version before: the header scrolled away with it, so after one step the reviewer was on a card with no way to the next but scrolling back up, and it said neither where it was nor went back. The design drew a full header and a compact one that sticks; one bar that is the header's last row keeps the pager's buttons in one place, where the reviewer's focus doesn't scroll away under them. The bar never wraps: below 1280px the stuck title goes and the threads' chip keeps its glyph and count, leaving the pager's title room, and below 640px the pager's title goes, leaving `‹ 1 of 3 ▾ ›`, its count before the first step drops the word, and Re-run and Show files keep their icons, named for screen readers; before the pager the bar already ran past its edge there. Its height is `--review-bar-h`, which the file cards' sticky headers, the tree rail and the page's `scroll-padding-top` read, so nothing sticks or takes the focus under it. Whether it's stuck comes from an `IntersectionObserver` on the bar with the window's top edge moved down a pixel. While the code's analysis runs, a progress strip of its stages sits under the bar; Claude's run has the hairline instead, since the reviewer waits on one thing, not six. The bar starts with the switch between the layouts, Code, Overview and, once there's a tour, Tour, then a divider; below 1280px it's their icons, named for screen readers and in a tooltip with `v`, which does the same. Map and Overview were a pair of buttons in the bar first, and went to the Display menu as a choice the reviewer makes once and keeps, which took room the pager's title needs. Switching turned out to be a step taken back and forth, a look at where the code sits and back to it, and in the menu it was two clicks each way with nothing on the page saying it was there. Each switch is an entry of the browser's history, the layout in the address, `?view=code`, `?view=overview` or `?view=tour`, so Back and Forward go between them, each keeping its place (see Between pages); the last one chosen is kept per browser, for a review opened without one. A review without a tour shows the overview where the address or the stored choice names the tour, and the address is changed to say so. Switching back from a layout opened by the switch, with nothing moved there, is Back: the overview's focus still on the box it opened on, or the tour's current step the one it landed on, puts the reader on the line they left. From the code opened from the overview or the tour, the switch, Esc and `v` go back to the entry it was opened from, and its box or step takes the focus. A second row under the bar, Back to overview or Back to tour, was the version before; it did what the switch above it does. A layout kept only per browser was the version before: Back left the review, and the overview and `v` back opened the first file of the directory in view, not the line the reader was on. The Display menu keeps the Tour switch. The layouts: The tree beside the code says where the code being read sits in the codebase: directories are the one part of its structure known without a checkout. It's drawn as the `hunk-filetree-v4` design has it, which took IntelliJ IDEA's project view for its model, since that's the tree the Java reviewers it was drawn for read all day. Every directory is a heading, a chain of directories with no files and one directory in it is one heading (`web/src`), and at the top a directory with no files and more than one directory in it is no heading, so it costs no indent on every row under it. Two or more headings in a row under such directories are a group: a muted caption says the directories once, `src/test/java/com/acmecorp/fulfillment/orders/`, and the headings under it, a level in, name only what's below it, `controllers` and `services/payment`. A heading alone keeps its whole path, as `substratevm/src/com.oracle.svm.core`, and stays at the top level, so it doesn't read as one of the group above it. Those directories before every heading's name was the version before: on the Java service fixture four headings began with the same 46 characters, wider than the rail, and its end, where they differed, was cut off. A heading or a caption too long for its row loses whole directories from its middle, `java/com/…/fulfillment/orders`, measured as a file name is. On the many-folder fixtures that's 2, 2 and 7 captions. A Java module's sources repeat its name, `com.oracle.svm.core/src/com/oracle/svm/core/pgo/`, and the tree leaves the repeat out, `com.oracle.svm.core/pgo`, the full path in the row's tooltip; `byTreePath` compares the paths as the tree shows them, so the cards keep the tree's order. A heading is a chevron, its folder's icon and its path, muted with its last directory in the text's color and medium weight, and a closed one says how many files it holds. Headings don't stick and have no guide line. The version before v4 had both, gave a directory of one file no heading, its row naming it (`routes/setup.tsx`), and said the directory every file is in once above the tree; on the many-folder fixtures that was 13, 9 and 22 headings for 24, 23 and 27 files, and v4's rules make them 18, 20 and 22. Before that, headings outnumbered files (23 for 24, 25 for 23, 35 for 27), and a flat list with a heading per directory had seven headings for delphi-code #2's seven files. The icons are IDEA's own New UI ones, unmodified, light and dark variants, vendored in `web/src/review/tree/icons/` with their Apache-2.0 license and provenance and listed in the package's notices: a Java file is a class, a Java test a class with IDEA's test mark, a deleted Java file Java's file type, since there's no class left, and other files their type's icon, `unknown` when IDEA's set as vendored has none (CSS, HTML, Go and others for now). A directory is a module when it's a dotted name with a `src/` in it, a package inside one or under a Java or Kotlin source root, else a folder. Every Java file shows the class icon: an interface's or an enum's would need prep to record each file's top-level type from tree-sitter, a contract change and a pipeline version bump that drops every cached AI run. Each icon is two images, the dark one shown under `.dark`, so the theme switches without a render; they're images rather than markup because their colors are the icons' own, which the tokens rule keeps out of our source. They carry no status, so the contrast check doesn't cover them. Lucide shapes by role, colored by language family, with a file-plus or file-minus for a new or deleted file, were the version before. A file's status is on its name, as IDEA colors changed files: a new file's name in the added lines' color, a deleted file's in the removed lines' color and struck through, a modified or renamed one in the text's color, and a new or deleted file's extension a muted mix of its color. A rename says "was" and its old name in the tooltip, and the row's accessible name says the status in words, with its type, lines, threads, findings and directory. On screen a new file is told from a modified one by its color alone, which in dark is 1.02:1 against the text, below the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.1 asks of a difference in color alone; the design was taken as it is, over ENGINEERING.md's rule that a status is never color alone, and so was the rename, which only the tooltip shows: the `renamed` chip was the version before. A file's row is its icon, its name and its marks: open threads, a dot in `severity-minor` for Claude's findings with their count above one, and its added and removed lines, a zero left out, in tints mixed toward muted. The dot is the design's, whatever the finding's severity; the design's ring for a risk went with the risks. A row never wraps: a name too long for it loses whole camel-case words from its middle, `Recurring…Support.java`, never its extension, measured with a canvas in the row's font whenever the rail's width changes; the version before wrapped the counts under the name, a line taller. - **Overview:** the changed directories as a layered diagram. A box is a directory: its path, its file count and its entries (routes, a page, a command), colored as mechanical when every change in it is. Its path is the tree's, without a Java module's repeat of its name, and one too long for the widest box loses whole directories from its middle, `src/test/java/…/orders/controllers/payments/`, as a tree heading does, the full path in its tooltip; a file's name loses words from its middle, never its extension. Cutting at the end was the version before: on a GraalVM PR every box began `substratevm/src/com.oracle.svm.core/src/com/o…` or `compiler/src/jdk.graal.compiler/src/jdk/graal…`, and the directories that told them apart were cut off. Geist Mono is 7.2 px a character at the label's size, where 8.6 was assumed. Directories nothing in the PR calls are on top, each one row below its lowest caller. Edges are the imports, calls, type uses and requests between the directories' files, merged into one per pair of boxes; one carrying a request is drawn apart, because it crosses into another process. Two directories that call each other keep the edge joining more pairs of files pointing down, and the other runs up the side; on a tie, or in a longer cycle, the edges into the directory a flow reads first run up, as for files. Tests and test helpers are badges on the directories they reach, and generated files are faded. A directory no edge touches and a test that reaches no changed code aren't drawn: the tree lists every file, and the overview is for how the changed code connects. Under the diagram were a strip of the directories, Not linked, and a list of the tests, Tests that call no changed code, before that; and before them each test was a box in its directory, which in Java, where tests are in another source root and rarely link to the code, made a box of each test directory: on graal #15134 four of the strip's seven. A legend above the diagram said what the boxes and lines mean, and a line under it named the hovered box's files, flows and edges; both went as text nobody read, and a box's name says the same to a screen reader. The directory of the file last in view in the code is outlined. A click on a box opens its first file in the map, and the switch, Esc and `v` there come back to it; a button on it opens it in place to its files, laid out by the same rules. A box says in how many places code outside the PR uses what its files change, “used in 4 places outside the PR”, tests aside; the uses themselves are on the code, under the map's “Used unchanged in”. Faded nodes for the files outside the PR, one row below the code they use with a dashed edge up into it, grouped by directory above 10, were the version before: on graal #15134 they were 11 of the diagram's 20 boxes and 17 of its 31 edges, and what they name is read where the code is. Rows by depth, ordered by their neighbors' positions, are enough at that size without a layout library. **The overview's preview forms.** The Display menu's Overview (preview) choice, kept per browser as `overview-form`, draws the overview as its data flow, the default, as its directories, or as one of three forms of the PR's flow paths ([DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) says why three). `flowPaths` in `web/src/pages/review/flow-paths.ts` is the pure function from the analysis to all three, importing only domain code as `fileOverview` does. A path starts at the entries of one of the code's flows, or else at the definitions of a file that no changed code calls, and runs what their definition calls reach (see [Deterministic prep](#2-deterministic-prep-no-model)): a file is a stop only where a definition the path runs is in it, so shared code is a stop on each path that runs it. Type uses aren't followed, and a request ends a path in the route it names without being followed, since the route has a path of its own. A path that starts at no entry isn't drawn when another runs every file on it: on graal #15134, 27 files have a definition that no changed code calls and that calls another, an override or a callback most of them, and 9 such paths are left. Starting at what each flow reads, its whole parts, was the version before. With definition calls it would have left out the PR's main path: `PGOInstrumentationFeature`'s `afterRegistration`, where GraalVM reaches the change, is in a class that isn't a flow's start, because other code reads one of its options. An analysis stored before the definition calls has its paths from the hints between parts. A file outside the PR starts no path: a stop that code outside uses says in how many places, with a glyph and a count, as a directory's box does. Each such file starting a path was the version before: on graal #15134, 13 of 19 rows, two of them the PR's own rows again but for a file or two. A path is a tree from the files it starts in: each stop is under the one of its callers fewest calls from the start, and names them all in its tooltip and its accessible name. `FlowPath.calls` holds the path's calls between files, every one a definition call, and no form draws a link that isn't one of them, which a test holds. A stop's order on a chain was the version before, the order a depth-first walk first reached the files in, with everything the flow lists after it: on graal #15134 34 of the rows' 99 arrows joined two files with no call between them, and `ProfileDumper` ended a row where nothing calls it. A file a flow only lists, by a type it names, is on no path. Paths that start in the same files, run the same ones and send the same requests are one path with each label: on delphi-code #2 its three routes. A stop is a file, new when the PR adds it; a file is code when it has a hunk no proof covers, isn't a test, a doc or generated, and is in a language megareviewer parses. The rest are listed by kind, and code no path runs is listed as on no path; a test holds that every changed file is on a path or in one of those lists. The lanes' columns are the stops' directories, each after the longest chain of calls between directories that reaches it, a call that closes a cycle not counting. Ordering them by where each path first reached them was the first version: on graal #15134 it put `Expander.java` right of the code it calls. `bowTie` in `flow-bow-tie.ts` puts a path on the left, standing for the files it starts in, the files that call another changed file or send a request in the middle by directory, and the rest on the right. Its links are the path's calls, one between two boxes of the middle going round their right side. A path linked to every box of its middle was the version before, whether or not its start calls it. A call back into the start isn't drawn, since nothing points left. A box of several files opens in place, by a button on it as the overview's directories do, to a box per file with that file's own links, and Collapse above the diagram closes it; the focus goes to the first of the files, or back to the box. A click on the closed box opened its first file and nothing reached the others, 24 of graal #15134's 29 files in boxes of several, which was the first version. The files as chips inside the box was the alternative: one control fewer, but the links would still be the directory's, so which of 13 files calls what stays unsaid, and a box that tall is no longer a bow tie. The page keeps what's opened, the lanes' unfolded cells too, so coming back from a file finds it there, and a closed box or a folded cell takes the focus for the files it holds. `FlowLanes` is a table, with the paths as row headers and the directories as column headers, and a cell with more than three files folds the rest behind a button, and the column of paths stays in view as the lanes scroll, except under 640px, where it would cover most of them. It draws no lines: one through a row's cells, which was the version before, joins every file in a cell to every file in the next, and the table has no place for a line from one chip to another. The stop with the pointer or the focus marks, on its row, the stops that call it and that it calls. `FlowBowTie` is buttons over an inline SVG, as the overview is. `FlowRows` is a list of trees: a stop that calls one other goes on along its line with a chevron for the call, and one that calls several has them under it, those that call nothing more on one line with no mark between them. A stop opens its first part in the map and Esc there comes back to it, as from a box of the overview. The stops are buttons in the Tab order, with no arrow keys: a preview isn't worth a keymap. With a tour, the tour's strip still groups by the overview's directories. In the map, each point is on the part its lines are in, or else on the first part of the hunks it rests on, and its kind says where on it. A finding is a card under the last line it rests on, as a thread is, with a bug in that line's number cell: its title, one muted line of its severity, in its color, and its type, its text, the mismatch it shows and its suggested change as a diff, then Dismiss, Edit and Add to review. Six things before the title were the version before: a Finding label, type, severity and Draft chips, the lines' reference and "Only you see this". The title is what the reviewer reads; Draft and "Only you see this" said one thing twice, which Add to review says a third time; and the reference repeated the mark on the number above the card, so it's left to a card that isn't under its lines. Added to the review, the draft takes its text and suggestion but not its type or severity, which were Claude's, and the card folds to a line above the draft that holds it, and comes back if that draft is discarded. A mismatch no finding names is the same card without either. The lines a point rests on are marked on their number beside the code: a tint, the number in its color and medium weight, and a 3 px rail on the code's side, the first point's where they overlap. The color is the finding's severity's, blocking red, major orange, minor amber, and grey for a mismatch; the card's bar, its severity's word, the bug and the landing's wash take it too, and a tour step's chips. The contrast check has each on every line tint. Every finding red was the version before, beside an amber severity chip that said it mattered little. The list the position opens is in the pager's order, each finding with its type and severity. A bar at the row's edge was the version before: about 115 px left of the code, it merged with the card's border and the focus bar, and on a range of one to three lines read as a tick. The edge bar is left to the focus and the open comment box. Two other forms were drawn and rejected: a caption line with a rail and no card, a fourth shape and quieter than something the reviewer is asked to check, and the lines themselves tinted with the note as their header, which replaces the diff's green or red on them. A point whose lines its part doesn't show sits under the part's header, and the other hunks a point rests on link to it, but not the other parts of the hunk its lines are in, which are around it. Dismiss folds a point to one line, with Undo. While risks and decisions were points, a risk was a lighter card of a finding's shell under its lines, with the test that checked it, and a decision a chip at the end of its line that opened a footnote (see DESIGN.md). Every point a card of one shape, with Raise and Dismiss, was the version before, first over its part and then under the last of its lines: on the fixture PR five cards sat on the receipt route, and the two findings read no louder than the three that could be left alone. A quiet list for risks and decisions under the findings' cards was tried and dropped: it kept all three kinds in one box. The designer's version had a teal band for logic code, a margin rail for decisions, Mark reviewed on risks and keys of their own; they were left out, for the reasons the page's elements record above. A tint under the code was the alternative to the mark: it would need a contrast pair for every syntax color on three more surfaces, for what a mark on the number beside a card that names its severity already says. Mechanical hunks are collapsed with their proof ("moved, verified identical"), and the user can expand them. A point guidance shaped says so on its card, in a line of its own: “From your preference:” and the rule, or “From REVIEW.md”, a link to the preferences page and not to the preference, which may have been edited or deleted since the run kept its words. A point a Don't flag preference left out is folded to one line where its card would be, “Left out by your preference: Naming”, with Show. Folded, it isn't a step, isn't in the chips' or the tree's counts and marks no lines; shown, it's the point's card and behaves as any point. Shown is the page's own state: a reload folds it again unless it was raised or dismissed, because a new run reuses `f1` and a stored “shown” would open a point the reviewer never saw. Going to a left-out point from a link shows it first. When every point was left out the bar says so, “Claude found nothing to raise, and left out 2 by your preferences”, rather than that nothing was found while folded lines sit in the code. Dismiss has a menu beside it with “Don't flag things like this…”, which opens a form on the card in place of its actions: the kind fixed, the rule prefilled with the point's title for the reviewer to word, the scope the PR's repository first. Saving adds the preference and dismisses the point. The usage line names what the run read, “Sonnet 5.5 through Claude Code with 2 preferences and REVIEW.md”, and Run details lists each preference as the run had it, each guideline file with its size, and how many points were left out.
files.DESIGN.md:
How code review should work now that most code is generated. See [MISSION.md](MISSION.md) for why.

- **Product form:** standalone web UI, served locally by a CLI, with no server of ours. See [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md).

- **An AI review follows what the reviewer values.** Request AI review said the same things to every reviewer: one who never wants a comment about naming got one on every PR, and one who cares most about tenant isolation had to hope Claude thought of it. megareviewer now keeps the reviewer's preferences, on their machine, and gives them to the passes. A preference is a rule, one short sentence, with a kind, **Look for** or **Don't flag**, a scope, everywhere or one repository, and a switch; a run reads the enabled ones for everywhere, then the PR's repository's. Free-text notes per scope, like a CLAUDE.md, were the alternative: a point couldn't then say which preference shaped it, and a learned proposal would be a line appended to prose. Global only leaks one codebase's rule into another; per repository only makes the reviewer write "no naming nits" in each. Preferences change what's flagged, and not the wording of comments: a comment posts under the reviewer's name, and they edit it before it does. They can't touch the safety rules: text in a PR aimed at an automated reviewer is still a finding, a mechanical proof is still the code's, and a path rule's contract still orders the flows.

  They come from three places. The reviewer writes them. A repository's guideline files, `REVIEW.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `.github/copilot-instructions.md` at its root, are detected, and the reviewer switches them: `REVIEW.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` are on unless switched off, since the code under review was written to the agents' instructions and the review should hold it to them, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `.github/copilot-instructions.md` off unless switched on, since the first is for people and can be long. Only `REVIEW.md` on was the version before: the agents' files, and every file they link, reached a review only for a reviewer who had found the switch. And megareviewer proposes rules from the reviewer's reviews, in two ways: at the point, where Dismiss has "Don't flag things like this", which opens a rule drafted from that point for the reviewer to word and save, with no model call; and on request, "Suggest from my reviews" on a repository, one model call over what megareviewer recorded the reviewer doing on its pull requests, the points they dismissed and raised and the comments they posted, and the reviewer's own comments on its host, each comment once. Two buttons were the version before, "Suggest from my reviews" over what was recorded in every repository and "Import from my past reviews" over one repository's host: they ended in the same proposals, and the first was disabled until megareviewer had recorded enough, which on a new install is every repository. Learned means proposed: megareviewer never turns what the reviewer did into a rule by itself. A proposal says what it would add and what it's based on, and the reviewer accepts it with Add, to edit it as any preference after, or rejects it with Dismiss; a rejected one isn't proposed again. Applying learned rules at once, with a page to remove them, was the alternative: a review that changed and didn't say why. Sending the model the last dismissed and raised points as examples was the other: nothing the reviewer can read or correct. A model call after every publish, and reading the host's history at the first review of a repository, were both rejected as requests and a model call nobody asked for, on the reviewer's plan. Everyone's comments on the host were the alternative to the reviewer's own: the team's habits, which aren't this reviewer's preferences. A proposal's words come from a model reading point titles, which come from PR text, so a PR could try to plant a rule; a proposal is only ever text the reviewer reads and accepts.

  A point says which preference shaped it, "From your preference: check tenant isolation" or "From REVIEW.md", and the mark stays right after the preference is edited or deleted, because the run keeps the guidance it was given. "Don't flag" folds, it doesn't hide: Claude still reports a finding such a preference matches, marked as left out, and the page shows it folded to one line with the preference and Show. Not reporting it was the alternative: cheaper, and the reviewer never learns what a rule removed, or that it's too wide. Keeping only the major and blocking ones was the other. A mark that doesn't check out, one naming a preference the run didn't have or "left out" by a Look for preference, is dropped, never the point: unsure, the page shows more. At most 50 preferences can be enabled per scope, and the 51st is refused with a message, since sending the first 50 of more would drop the rest silently; for the same reason a guideline file that doesn't fit the prompt isn't cut but left to be read, or left out where nothing reads it, and the page says so.

- **A repository's rules are its guideline files and the files they link.** A root `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` is often an index: megareviewer's own is 310 bytes and names the documents with the rules in them. So megareviewer finds a repository's **harness**: the five guideline files and, from each, what it imports (`@docs/rules.md`), links in Markdown or names in prose, a `.md`, `.mdc`, `.markdown` or `.txt` file of the repository's, or a folder, which brings the Markdown under it. A folder is named as often as a file: graal's `AGENTS.md` says documentation lives under `docs/`, and pytorch's `CLAUDE.md` names `torch/distributed/` before the `AGENTS.md` in it. A code span that holds a path and nothing else names it, since those two are both in code spans; a fence and a span with more in it are examples, as every code span was in the first version, which caught neither. Outside a Markdown link a folder ends in a slash, so `I/O`, `before/after` and a branch's name are no folders. Every file named is walked before a folder brings any, so a folder of a thousand files crowds out no file a guideline links: graal's 14 suites, each named as a folder, filled the 200 files at the first hop and left out 53 docs that files further from the root link by name. A folder's `.txt` files are left out, since in one they're licenses and notices more often than rules. Every Markdown file in the repository was the alternative: of megareviewer's 104 that adds the eval cases' fixture files and each adapter's `PROVENANCE.md`, which are nobody's rules.
